**Riverton Opens Solar-Powered Microgrid to Cut Energy Costs and Improve Outage Resilience**

*RIVERTON, March 9, 2026* — The City of Riverton switched on a new solar-powered microgrid Monday, a project officials say will reduce municipal electricity costs and help keep critical services running during regional power outages.

The microgrid, built on the grounds of the Riverton Water Treatment Facility, combines a 6.2-megawatt solar array with a 14-megawatt-hour battery system. City engineers said the system can “island” from the main grid during emergencies, maintaining power for the treatment plant as well as a nearby fire station and an emergency shelter.

Mayor Elena Park called the project “a practical investment” that will pay for itself over time. “This is about reliability and affordability,” Park said at a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by city staff, utility representatives and local residents. “When the larger grid is strained—whether from storms or heat waves—Riverton will be better positioned to keep essential operations online.”

According to the city’s public works department, the project cost $18.4 million and was financed through a mix of municipal bonds, a state clean-energy grant and a power purchase agreement for a portion of the solar output. The city estimates annual savings of roughly $1.1 million in avoided energy purchases and peak-demand charges, though officials cautioned that savings will vary with weather and market conditions.

Riverton Utilities spokesperson Daniel Ortiz said the microgrid is designed to coordinate with the broader distribution network, exporting power during periods of high solar generation and charging batteries when electricity prices are lower. “It’s not just about producing power; it’s about managing it intelligently,” Ortiz said.

Some residents raised questions about maintenance costs and end-of-life disposal of battery components. Public works director Marina Shah said the city’s contract requires the vendor to provide long-term performance guarantees and a recycling plan. “We built lifecycle responsibility into the procurement,” Shah said.

City officials said the microgrid will be monitored for the next 12 months as part of a performance verification period, with quarterly reports to the city council. If targets are met, Riverton plans to evaluate similar installations at the municipal hospital and a cluster of schools that serve as designated emergency cooling centers.
